newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel reopens Hebron road after three years.
newsitem.headline: Israel reopens Hebron road after three years.

text.p: Israel partly reopened a main road in the West Bank town of Hebron to limited Palestinian traffic on Monday for the first time since a 1994 massacre of Arabs by a Jewish settler.
A U.S.-brokered peace deal paved the way for Palestinian ambulances, taxis and municipal vehicles to travel along a section of Shuhada, or Martyrs, street again -- albeit in only one direction.
Cars with Israeli licence plates had free run of the road, up and down a heavily guarded hilly stretch bordering a Moslem cemetery in an area of Hebron still under Israeli control.

Hours after the reopening, journalists and Israeli soldiers outnumbered vehicles plying the route that begins at an outdoor market and ends at a "no-entry" sign which Israeli authorities placed at a turnoff to a Jewish seminary.
Israeli and Palestinian workers cleared roadblocks on Sunday night, but the more formidable barrier of mistrust remained.

"It is a new reality, a problematic reality," settler spokesman Noam Arnon told Israel Television minutes before the opening. "It will be flooded with Arab cars which will pose a real danger to the Jews here."
For some Palestinian taxi drivers it was only more of the same in the volatile town where some 400 Jewish settlers live or study amidst more than 100,000 Arabs.

Israeli policemen, wearing flak jackets and carrying assault rifles, banned Palestinian taxis from parking outside newly reopened taxi offices, saying permission had yet to be granted by Israeli military authorities.
"He can park here but he won't have a car left," one police officer said to another, pointing at a taxi driver. "They know the rules."

Israeli authorities said the street, closed to Palestinian vehicles since Jewish settler Baruch Goldstein massacred 29 Arab worshippers at al-Ibrahimi mosque in February 1994, would reopen in stages over a four-month period.
Hebron's Palestinian mayor Mustafa al-Natsheh demanded Israel step up the pace.
"It was agreed upon that (traffic) must move in the two directions and I see that they opened it for one direction," he told reporters.
For a brief moment in the morning, nothing moved on the street as a garbage truck blocked the road to pick up a dumpster.

Arab and Jew were caught in the same jam: a religious Jewish boy on a mountain bike, an armoured Israeli bus carrying settlers, an Arab taxi, an Israeli police car and Arab vegetable carts pulled by horses -- their bells jingling.
The street is likely to be on the agenda when Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meet on Thursday to iron out various disputes.

Other Palestinian demands include the release of prisoners, an easing of restrictions on the flow of people and goods between Israel and the Palestinian territories, clearance for a Gaza airport to open and work to start on a Gaza seaport.
On Shuhada street, Mustafa Jabari reopened his musty Hebron Travel Taxi office for the first time since the road was closed three years ago.
"We want to take people to Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo from here," he said, looking towards the future as he stepped into a time warp.
Jabari pointed to a dusty calendar still hanging on the wall. The year read 1994.
